pr_title: GDScript: Fix `MIN_INT` not representable as numeric literal
pr_body:
This PR fixes the inability to write the minimum `int` value as `-9223372036854775808` literal (in master this causes an error, but you can write `1 << 63` instead). This is now a literal, not a "unary minus and a number" expression.

Closes #42289.

Related: #48745.
pr_comments: `Expression` also has this issue (https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/42289#issuecomment-698565791). Should I fix it in this PR?

> `Expression` also has this issue ([#42289 (comment)](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/42289#issuecomment-698565791)). Should I fix it in this PR?

No, AFAIK, `Expression` is found in `core/math/expression.h`. You should create a new PR. Ping me in the chat with the PR, I'll set the 4.1 milestone to it.

issue_context.title: Bitwise operators OR and AND are not working with `-(2^63 - 1)` in 3.2.3 [regression]
issue_context.body:
<!-- Please search existing issues for potential duplicates before filing yours:
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues?q=is%3Aissue
-->

**Godot version:**
<!-- Specify commit hash if using non-official build. -->
3.2.3

**OS/device including version:**
<!-- Specify GPU model, drivers, and the backend (GLES2, GLES3, Vulkan) if graphics-related. -->
Windows 10, 2004

**Issue description:**
<!-- What happened, and what was expected. -->
Bitwise operators OR and AND aren't working 100% correctly in version 3.2.3, but were working in 3.2.2.

I didn't test XOR.

**Steps to reproduce:**

If I want to set bit 63 on a 64-bit int using:
var value:int = 0 | -9223372036854775808
I get -9223372036854775807 which is wrong
Godot just set bit 63 and bit 0!

Likewise, if I want to test for bit 63:
var value:int = -1 & -9223372036854775808
I get again -9223372036854775807 which is wrong
Godot tested bit 63 and bit 0!

(I also tested with Python, just to be sure)

Possibly related, I repeatedly see on the console while editing:

_ERROR: Cannot represent 9223372036854775808 as 64-bit integer, provided value is too big.
   At: core/ustring.cpp:1821_

Which is actually correct. However, I don't have that number anywhere in code. Well, I do have that number, but negative. The parser seems to be ignoring the minus sign.

My hunch is that "-9223372036854775808" is being incorrectly parsed, leading to incorrect bitwise operations.

**Minimal reproduction project:**
<!-- A small Godot project which reproduces the issue. Drag and drop a zip archive to upload it. -->
comments:
> Minimal reproduction project:

[Bitwise huge values.zip](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/files/5274311/Bitwise.huge.values.zip)

Indeed the issue seems to be that -9223372036854775808 is parsed as `-(9223372036854775808)`, and `9223372036854775808` is out of bounds for a signed 64-bit integer.

The same issue happens in 3.2.2 too if you use actual hexadecimal notation, which makes those magic numbers somewhat easier to parse. `-0x8000000000000000` fails as `hex_to_int64` is called on `0x8000000000000000`.

It's also reproducible in the `master` branch.

In `3.2`, the regression happened between `3.2.2-stable` and 3.2.3-beta1 (89f57ae12244f3269c9e3fe4684e16ec1fd2c989).

Probably caused by #40009 / #40149 (@mrushyendra).

> The same issue happens in 3.2.2 too if you use actual hexadecimal notation, which makes those magic numbers somewhat easier to parse. `-0x8000000000000000` fails as `hex_to_int64` is called on `0x8000000000000000`.

To clarify, that one is a pre-existing bug not caused by the above PRs. But that's also something that should be fixed eventually.

If I'm understanding correctly, it seems like the issue is not with the changes in #40009 itself, but due to `String::to_int64` being called with the sign omitted when parsing? In that case, it seems like the choices are (i) doing away with the overflow checks and leaving such behavior undefined, or (ii) modifying the calls to `to_int64` when parsing

Yeah I think this might need to be fixed in the GDScript parser so that it calls `String::to_int64("-9223372036854775808")` instead of `String::to_int64("9223372036854775808")` and then making it negative.

This would fix both the current "regression" and the pre-existing bug when using `-0x8000000000000000` (with `hex_to_int64`).

CC @godotengine/gdscript

> Yeah I think this might need to be fixed in the GDScript parser

`Expression`s also have the same behavior, e.g this crashing test case have to use `(-9223372036854775807 - 1)` for the same reason - https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/40955#discussion_r464004709

> My hunch is that "-9223372036854775808" is being incorrectly parsed, leading to incorrect bitwise operations.

`-9223372036854775808` is **not** a literal, it's a unary minus of `9223372036854775808` which is not representable, the maximum `int` value is `9223372036854775807`. For the same reason, negative numbers in annotations did not work (#41183), before support for constant expressions was added.

This is somewhat of an argument in favor of handling negative number literals in the tokenizer, but it can lead to the problem of parsing expressions like `1-1` (binary minus without spaces). I'm not sure if it's worth it, since only one valid integer has the representability problem. You can use `1 << 63` instead.

review_comments:
I encountered the same problem in the highlighter, and the line of code for it winded up being

```gdscript
if (word == "true" || word == "false" || word == "null" || word == "PI" || word == "TAU" || word == "INF" || word == "NAN" || word == "self" || word == "super" || !reserved_keywords.has(word)
```
not so much in terms of correctness of syntax, but with the rule that if the previous word represents a value, it should be followed by a binary OP. For `super` it was more so because I decided to treat `.` like an operator too as it was helpful to determine when to highlight it like a number.

Maybe there's something to learn from this implementation, and maybe this function in the tokenizer can eventually be used in the highlighter instead of that long condition?

I've also noticed that the highlighter doesn't properly handle newlines and line continuations (for example, the `&&` operator doesn't always highlight correctly). Note that after the `NEWLINE` token, `+` must be treated as unary operator or the start of a numeric literal. But if it is a line continuation or multiline mode is enabled, then `+` can be binary operator.

I think for highlighter you can just keep a parentheses stack and flag if the current line is a continuation. Although with lambdas it can be difficult.

![](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/47700418/219283180-d10b1dad-1350-434b-96a6-ec5e435366f8.png)

The highlighter works line by line rn and idk how to fix it. This also messes with the highlighting of much more than just operators that can be unary or binary.

What I'm saying, maybe in the future we can use the tokenizer's info for this too. And also, some of the checks aren't consistent between our implementations, so I wanted to explain my motivation for them.

This is not obvious due to the fact that the first character of the number literal is consumed before the `number()`. I would prefer `number()` to be called when the current character is the first character of the numeric literal, whatever it is (`+`, `-`, `.`, `0` or some other digit).
